planting.note: Sow after last frost once soil is warm; white proso is the pale, food-grade seed class preferred for birdseed blends and home milling over the red or golden proso types.

directions: Drill or broadcast seed about 1/2 inch deep into warm, weed-free soil and thin stands to 4-6 inches apart; white proso is the pale-hulled market class grown for birdseed and human food rather than wildlife plots, and buyers pay a premium for clean, unmixed white seed lots. The plant tillers moderately and produces a loose, drooping panicle that ripens unevenly from the top down, so watch for shattering once the lower seeds harden. Cut whole stalks when most of the panicle has turned from green to straw color, then finish drying the bundles under cover for 10-14 days before threshing and winnowing. Because proso millet is one of the shortest-season grains available, a second planting is often possible in zones with a long enough frost-free window.

common_name: Red Proso Millet (Golden Proso, Wildlife Food Plot Type)

planting.note: Sow after last frost once soil is warm; red (golden) proso is the seed class most commonly planted for dove fields and wildlife food plots rather than for human food.

directions: Broadcast or drill seed roughly 1/2 inch deep into a warm, firm seedbed; red (also sold as golden) proso millet carries a reddish-brown hull and is the standard seed class planted for dove and quail food plots across the central and southern United States because the ripe seed heads are highly attractive to game birds. The open panicles mature unevenly and drop seed readily once dry, which is an advantage for wildlife feeding but means home growers harvesting for their own use should cut stalks as soon as the majority of seed hardens rather than waiting for full uniform ripeness. Bundle and hang stalks to finish drying for about two weeks, then thresh over a tarp and winnow in a light breeze. This type tolerates poor, droughty soils and heat better than most other summer grains, making it a reliable choice for a quick warm-season planting.

common_name: Golden Flax (Yellow-Seeded Oilseed and Culinary Flax)

planting.note: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, up to the last frost date; golden flax needs cool weather to establish and struggles once summer heat arrives.

directions: Broadcast seed thickly over a firm, weed-free bed and rake in to about 1/4 inch, since golden flax relies on dense stands to keep its slender stems from lodging. This yellow-seeded type is grown specifically for the table — the mild, nutty flaxseed is favored for grinding into meal for baking and smoothies over the more assertive brown-seeded types. Watch the sky-blue flowers give way to round seed capsules, and cut whole plants at the base once most capsules have dried to a tan color and rattle when shaken. Dry the cut bundles under cover for one to two weeks before threshing by flailing or treading, then winnow thoroughly, as golden seed shows any chaff more readily than brown flax.

common_name: Brown Flax (Traditional Oilseed and Fiber Flax)

planting.note: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, up to the last frost date; brown flax is the traditional oilseed color type and shares the same cool-season culture as other flax.

directions: Broadcast seed onto a firm, fine seedbed and rake in lightly to about 1/4 inch deep, sowing thickly so plants support each other against wind and rain. Brown flax is the older, more widely grown oilseed color type worldwide, with a stronger, earthier flavor than golden flax and a long history of use for both pressed oil and fiber where stands are allowed to grow taller and thinner. Harvest by pulling or cutting whole plants once the lower third of the stem has yellowed and most seed capsules have turned brown and dry, then shock the bundles upright to finish curing for about two weeks. Thresh over a tarp or inside a barrel and screen the seed carefully, since brown flaxseed is oily and can clump if stored before it is fully dry.

planting.note: Sow after last frost once soil is warm; ivory teff is the pale, mild-flavored seed class used for lighter-colored injera and other food-grade teff products.

directions: Mix the dust-fine seed with dry sand for even coverage and surface-broadcast onto a firm, rolled seedbed, pressing lightly rather than covering, since ivory teff germinates poorly if buried. This is the pale-seeded food-grade class prized for producing lighter-colored injera and for grinding into a mild flour, in contrast to the stronger flavor of brown teff. Cut whole plants near the base once most of the fine seed heads have turned from green to golden-tan but before shattering begins in wind, then finish drying under cover for a week or more. Thresh gently by beating bundles over a smooth tarp and winnow in the lightest possible breeze, as the tiny ivory seed is easily lost.

planting.note: Sow after last frost once soil is warm; brown teff is the traditional reddish-brown seed class most widely grown in Ethiopia and prized for its deeper, more robust flavor.

directions: Blend the minuscule seed with dry sand or fine compost before broadcasting onto a firm, well-prepared bed, then roll or tamp lightly instead of covering with soil. Brown teff carries the deeper reddish-brown seed coat and stronger, tangier flavor traditionally used for classic sour injera, and is generally the hardier, more widely adapted seed class for home growers experimenting with teff outside its native highlands. Its fine tillers form an airy stand that should be cut at the base once the majority of seed heads have dried to a rusty brown, well before a hard rain can shatter the crop. Dry the cut bundles under cover for a week or more, then thresh by gentle flailing and winnow in a light, steady breeze to separate the small heavy seed from the chaff.
